title: Billy Porter and Hannah John-Kamen Join The Colour of My Skin as Producers
excerpt:
Billy Porter and Hannah John-Kamen have joined the producing team of the short film The Colour of My Skin.
Co-directed by Anuparna Roy and Amar Singh, the completed shoot explores love, racial identity and the legacy of colonialism.
body_md:
Production has wrapped on The Colour of My Skin, a short film bringing together two filmmakers whose work spans cinema, visual art and social activism. Billy Porter and Hannah John-Kamen have joined the project as producers alongside Stephanie Faucher and Jordan Dykstra. Studio Á, the art and film venture co-founded by Dykstra and Amar Singh, is also involved. The announcement comes as the film moves into post-production rather than announcing a release date.

The film is co-directed by Anuparna Roy and British-Indian artist and activist Amar Singh. Singh wrote the screenplay and appears on screen with Efeosa Jordan Afolabi and Namita Lal. Its central characters are Avi, a British-Indian artist preparing to exhibit his work at an art salon, and Darius, a Black musician with whom Avi shares a complicated romantic history. Their renewed encounter brings ambition, intimacy and unresolved tensions into the same space.

Rather than treating race and colonial history solely as abstract political subjects, the filmmakers aim to explore how those histories shape personal relationships. The story examines racial identity, equality and the sometimes uncomfortable distance between the principles people champion publicly and their conduct toward those closest to them. The available synopsis establishes those themes without revealing the full narrative or its ending.

Singh developed the project from his poem of the same name, which addresses colonial legacies, racial inequality, displacement and the desire to belong. Through his London gallery, he has sought to give greater visibility to women, minority artists and LGBTQ+ creators overlooked by established institutions. His activism has also included work supporting the decriminalization of homosexuality in India and efforts to improve women's rights and representation within cultural organizations. For Singh, the film turns those outward-facing concerns into a question about the consistency of private behavior and public ideals.

The collaboration reunites Singh and Roy after her second feature, Lovers in the Blue Night, on which Singh served as an associate producer. That film won the Netpac Award for best Asian film at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Roy had previously won the Horizons directing prize at Venice in 2025 for her debut feature, Songs of Forgotten Trees, becoming the first Indian filmmaker to receive that directing honor. Her involvement gives the new short a notable connection to recent international festival recognition.

Sunil Borkar served as cinematographer, while Maximillian Raynor designed the costumes. The production announcement was made around WAVES Film Bazaar, the industry market associated with the International Film Festival of India in Goa. No festival premiere, public release or streaming launch has been confirmed. Porter and John-Kamen's participation is in producing roles; the announcement does not identify them as cast members.
